items.title: Harold Mabern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 31, 2010
items.q: I mean everybody knows how I feel about Ahmad and Phineas, that those are my two favorite piano players bar none

ctx.x: But you had this interest in bebop, and where did that come from at that age? Was it by the radio or buying LPs?

No, see that’s the thing. On the radio you didn’t hear no — first of all, on the radio you would hear maybe some Dave Brubeck and some George Shearing, but you didn’t really hear no Art Tatum, Charlie Parker, Bud Powell, at that time because that was too strong © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-

for the airways. So even then, the artists who played that way had to play in a more commercial-type vein. But we always had big bands that would come to Memphis, like the Count Basie big band, or the Duke Ellington big band, or the Lionel Hampton Orchestra and they would play it at the Palace Theater and on that group would be like a big band, a jazz vocalist, maybe Sarah Vaughan or Ella Fitzgerald or something like that, and a comedian, and that would be it. items.title: Harold Mabern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 31, 2010
items.q: Phineas Newborn Jr. had two pianos, both of them were bad.

ctx.x: What were the pianos like that you got to play on?

Very bad. I mean really bad. See you know I think that probably most of the great piano players that would want to came up. Art Tatum played on bad pianos. Phineas Newborn Jr. had two pianos, both of them were bad. So there were no Steinways during that time. As a matter of fact they were all uprights. Very bad, keys missing, ivories jagged so if you’re not careful you’d cut your finger. Oh that was some bad times. But we had to deal with what we had. And a lot of times the pianos would be so out of tune, that’s…
